utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The accused can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is the case number IT-01-47-PT, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic, Mehmed Alagic, and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, counsel. For the Prosecution, appear Madam Bodson, Senior Trial Attorney; Ms. Cynthia Fairweather, Legal Officer; and myself, Ekkehard Withopf, OTP trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, attorney from Sarajevo, and together with Mr. John Jones, we are appearing on behalf of General Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, attorney from Sarajevo, representing Mr. Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Additional one question to the accused: Do you all understand the proceedings in a language you understand, and especially today, are you all in a condition to follow these proceedings with regard to a medical examination? THE ACCUSED KUBURA: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED ALAGIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can hear three times yes. Thank you. Additionally, we have the honour of the presence of the same representatives of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as of today, Mr. Dzihanovic and Mr. Limov. Once again, I take the opportunity to emphasise that this Tribunal highly appreciates your cooperation with the ICTY under the Rules of the United Nations as friends of this Court. The Trial Chamber is still and only seized today with three motions on provisional release in application of Rule 65. Yesterday we heard the exhaustive submissions of the parties and statements by the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina and statements of the three accused. A basis of facts was established, enabling the Trial Chamber to come to a possible decision. Only as regards possible guarantees, different views were exchanged. The purpose of this hearing today, therefore, is restricted to the evaluation of these guarantees. In terms of the principle of proportionality, are the guarantees necessary themselves? -- a question which might be challenged by the Defence. Are they seen as on the whole sufficient to meet the expectations set out in Rule 65? To this latter point, there might be a submission by the Office of the Prosecutor. She indicated already yesterday that the guarantees in principle are regarded - I quote from page 79 of the transcript - "relevant and sufficient in practice." Today it is only to assess the concrete guarantees as submitted today. And I take it as given that you had at least the opportunity to read the guarantees submitted. Therefore, I would invite you to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, to avoid any misunderstanding, I want to stress from the outset that the Prosecutor maintains her submission that the motion for provisional release regarding all three of the accused be denied. It is the strong opinion of the Prosecutor that the recital of yesterday's submissions do not give any reason to change her point of view. With regard to the conditions as detailed in the Court document the Prosecutor received early this afternoon, the Prosecution notes that some of the conditions are not as strict as requested by the Prosecutor; however, some others are even stricter. The Prosecutor notes that these conditions include a reporting obligation of the accused to the local police only once a week, instead of once a day as requested by the Prosecutor. The Prosecution submits that such a reporting regime is not strict enough to keep close control on whether the accused fulfil their obligation to remain within the confines of Sarajevo or Sanski Most respectively. The Prosecutor furthermore notes that the accused provided provisional release will be granted, should not seek access to documents and archives. The Prosecutor submits that such a condition needs to be far more detailed to avoid any potential misinterpretation. Finally, with regard to the conditions, the Prosecutor submits that some of the conditions are difficult to control as, for example, the condition to not have any contacts with victims and potential witnesses. For clarification purposes, the Prosecution submits that a further condition should be imposed, namely the condition that the accused should not instruct third persons to have such a contact to victims and potential witnesses. In this respect - and I understand that is an issue that has not yet or at least not yet sufficiently addressed in yesterday's hearing - the Prosecutor stresses that provisional release, if granted, would send the wrong signal to both the victims of the crimes the accused are charged with and the International Community. The victims of the crimes the accused are held responsible for consider the crimes as being serious, as does expressly the Prosecutor. It is not sufficient just to quote the heading of the crimes assets out in the Tribunal's Statute. Obviously, the accused are not charged with genocide. However, it is necessary to review the concrete crimes the accused are charged with, and these crimes are: Murder, wilful killing, violence to life and person, wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health, unlawful confinement of civilians, and some more. There is no doubt that these crimes are to be considered as serious ones. In addition, these crimes were committed over a long period of time and on several locations. In this regard, the Prosecution expressly appreciates the comments made by the Presiding Judge yesterday that the fact that the accused are only charged with their responsibility in terms of Article 7(3) of the Statute does not play a significant role. In addition, with all due respect, the Prosecutor still doubts whether the Trial Chamber is sufficiently aware of the impact of a decision granting provisional release on the relationship between Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia. The Prosecutor therefore wishes to announce that if the Trial Chamber grants provisional release, she intends to appeal the decision and expressly applies for a stay of the decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. We heard this. May I ask a question as concerns the guarantees? Am I right in referring to the transcript that you regarded yesterday the guarantees as sufficient, and on the other hand, suggested to have a restriction to the area or to the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina only? And I don't understand correctly when you now say it would be necessary to visit a police office once a day and not once a month. I see some discrepancy. Could you please explain this. The other points were easy to understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's also easy to explain. I think a reporting system ensuring that the accused report each day to a local police station ensures that they -- even when they are allowed to travel within the confines of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they will have to return each day back to their local town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic and General Hadzihasanovic in person support fully all the measures and guarantees that have been signed and which this Trial Chamber is being offered. If our motion is granted for my client, General Hadzihasanovic, to be provisionally released, I would appeal to the Trial Chamber simply that this point (h) under which my client has no access to documents or archives, that that should not be interpreted as prohibiting his counsel from having access to those archives, because in that case, his Defence would not be able to work properly. In other words, that the Defence does have access to those archives but not the accused Hadzihasanovic himself. In connection with the submissions made by my learned friend representing the OTP, I would just like to say a few words in response; namely, the Prosecutor should have a consistent position with regard to assessing the conditions under which it accepts guarantees and agrees to provisional release. Any reservations on the part of the Prosecution after the observations that you yourself have made regarding the cooperation between Bosnia-Herzegovina and this Tribunal, I do not think is appropriate, as that same Prosecution in previous cases has allowed the accused to go, for instance, to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, where some persons accused in public indictments are still living and have not been surrendered. In that case, the Prosecution itself agreed with provisional release. As to the seriousness of the crimes referred to by the Prosecution, in addition to what I said before, I think it is very important that the Prosecution realises that my client and the others have not been charged with genocide, and the Prosecution has agreed to provisional release of a person charged with genocide. Finally, I should like to refer back to your observations, Mr. President, when you said that we had to observe the principle of proportionality. The conditions must be such as to make sure that my client will come back to this Tribunal and will not be a threat to victims or witnesses. Those conditions, and especially those requested by the Prosecution today, should not constitute punishment for my client. Therefore, it is up to you to decide between guarantees for appearance in court and what might already be considered as a punishment for my client. That is why I am quite confident, Your Honours, that given the guarantees given to you, you will grant our motion for the provisional release of General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to avoid any further delays, the concrete question: Would it be an obstacle, from your point of view, to, in case provisional release would be granted, to order that your client should show up at the office of the police once a day?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that would not be a problem at all. He could report. But I feel that that is more than essential for my client to be trusted that he will appear in court when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. called. But I am absolutely in your hands, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. I'd like to start by just dealing with the final point made by the Prosecution, namely, the indication that they would be -- if you were minded to grant the applications of provisional release, that they will be applying for a stay, a stay of execution of your judgement. And to deal with that, firstly, I'm, frankly, rather surprised that the Prosecution hasn't drawn your attention, as they really should have done, to a sub-rule which in fact precludes that very application which they're making. If I could draw your attention to Rule 65(E), which states very clearly there: "The Prosecutor may apply for a stay of a decision by the Trial Chamber to release an accused on the basis that the Prosecutor intends to appeal the decision, and shall make such an application at the time of filing his or her response to the initial application for provisional release by the accused." The Rule couldn't be more clear. The Prosecution knows the Rules very well. They filed their response to the applications on the 28th of November, 2001, in the case of General Alagic. It was a full ten-page response after having taken the full 14 days to reply, but there is no mention there whatsoever that they would intend to seek a stay of any decision toward a provisional release, nor at any time since they have mentioned that, nor did they mention that at yesterday's hearing. So I would submit that that is enough to dispose of that matter. If we come back to that later, I will be very glad to address you as to the merits of any application for stay. But I would point out, first of all, that that is completely precluded from the Rules, which are absolutely clear on the matter. Just four comments in reply as to the conditions. Equally I would submit with Ms. Residovic it's possible, of course, for the General Alagic to report to a police station every day, but when one considers this over a period of months, it really does seem excessive to have to report to the police every day, particularly since the conditions already provide for spot-checks in essence, condition (e), "occasional unannounced visits" to the accused. That, taken in conjunction with the weekly reporting, I would submit, is sufficient to ensure that the accused will never be far from his home. As regards the second point which the Prosecution made about the accused should not seek -- sorry, that -- the condition not to seek access to documents in archives is not specific enough - I believe that was the objection - indeed it is fairly broad. We thought of adding to that condition "not to seek access to documents in archives pertinent to this case." If that's what the Prosecution is seeking, then we can add something of that nature. Equally, the condition which the Prosecution asks for, not to instruct third persons to have contact with victims and witnesses, that seems reasonable. I think we could agree to that. But the final point which the Prosecution made, while seeming to waver between agreeing to conditions and challenging the whole notion of provisional release, the Prosecution submitted again that this provisional release would send the wrong signal to the victims of the crimes. Well, Your Honour, that is true of every single case before this Tribunal. Every case has victims and witnesses, and if that were a -- if that were an objection to provisional release, it would never be granted. Unless I can assist you further, Your Honour, those are my submissions. We otherwise, obviously, consider that the conditions and guarantees are fully acceptable and that's why they were signed by us and by the representatives of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Please take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Kubura accepts in their entirety all the measures provided for, and they will be fulfilled and adhered to should the request for provisional release be granted. As to the rest, the Kubura Defence completely agrees with what the Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic and Alagic have stated already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, also to the surprise for this Trial Chamber, the issue of possibly applying for a stay of a decision arose today, and I would invite to the Prosecutor to add some facts or legal remarks with regard to Rule 65(E) justifying this new approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I want to address the observations made by my learned colleague Mr. Jones. He's right in addressing the issue of Rule 65(E); however, I disagree with his conclusions. Rule 65(E), in the opinion of the Prosecution, only precludes a request for a stay of a decision if an oral hearing is not schedule. Meanwhile, an oral hearing has been scheduled, and the situation changed. It's a new situation, and the Prosecutor is of the opinion that she now can request such a stay of a decision. And I want to inform the Trial Chamber that this is a clear order of the Prosecutor herself to request such a stay of a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please explain what is exactly the new situation since yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There were several submissions made, and the Prosecutor is of the opinion that even if this strict regime of conditions is put on the accused, it doesn't 100 per cent ensure that they will not flee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the conditions and the guarantees included in the documents now are going far beyond that what was indicated by the Prosecutor yesterday? And could you please give us some advice what is the new factual basis changing your view from yesterday when all these issues were deliberated very carefully?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, with regard to the condition to report only once a week, the Prosecutor is of the opinion that this condition makes it very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is not the point. The point is: I had the impression you wanted to make us believe that there is a new situation because we have a new set of guarantees, and I wanted to make it quite clear that these guarantees are stricter than the ones asked for by the Office of the Prosecutor, and I believe some submission has to be made from your side how it is possible that these more restrictive guarantees provide a new situation for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I appreciate your comments, and I want to inform you the only reason why we request such a stay of decision is order of the Prosecutor herself. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other submissions? Mr. Jones, you said you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would simply observe that as regards this distinction involving the fact that there was an oral hearing, there is no basis whatsoever in Rule 65 for that distinction. As regards the merits of granting a stay, I would prefer to wait, I think, until we reach that moment, if we get there. As I say, I think it should be sufficient to dispose of the application for a stay, the plain words of Rule 65(E), and it would only be if Your Honour were to find that there was still scope for argument that I would address you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Tribunal stands adjourned for one hour. We'll meet again at 6.30. --- Break taken at 5.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The accused can be brought in. Please be seated. The Trial Chamber has come to the conclusion that there are three decisions necessary because there are three motions, and we have to decide on an individual basis. To facilitate the proceedings, I will refer to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those parts of the decisions they have in common, the following guidelines. It says: This Trial Chamber of the International Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the former Yugoslavia since 1991, being seized of three motions for provisional release pursuant to the Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, hereby grants the applications and orders the provisional release of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Mehmed Alagic, and Amir Kubura on the following terms and conditions: The accused shall be transported to Schiphol airport in the Netherlands by the Dutch authorities. At Schiphol airport, the accused shall be provisionally released into the custody of the designated officials of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who shall accompany the accused for the remainder of their travel to Bosnia and Herzegovina and their respective place of residence; this will be Sarajevo for Enver Hadzihasanovic and Armin Kubura, and Sanski Most for Mr. Alagic. On their return flight, the accused shall be accompanied by a designated official or more of Bosnia-Herzegovina who shall deliver the accused into the custody of the Dutch authorities at Schiphol airport at a date and time to be determined by the Trial Chamber, and the Dutch authorities shall then transport the accused back to the Detention Unit. During the period of their provisional release, the accused shall abide by the following conditions, and the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall ensure compliance with such conditions: (a) to report within three days of their arrival the address to which the accused will be staying to the Registrar of the Tribunal and to indicate any change of address to the Registrar within three days of the change;. (b) to surrender their passport to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina; (c) to remain within the confines of Sarajevo for Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura, and of Sanski Most for Mr. Alagic; (d) to report once a week to the local police in Sarajevo for Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura, and in Sanski Most for Mehmed Alagic; (e) to consent to having officials of Bosnia-Herzegovina check with the local police about their presence and to the making of occasional unannounced visits to the accused by these officials or by a person designated by the Registrar of the Tribunal; (f) not to have any contacts with any other co-accused in the case; (g) not to have any contact whatsoever or in any way interfere with victims or potential witnesses or otherwise interfere in any way with the proceedings of the administration of justice; (h) not to seek access to documents and archives; (i) not to discuss their case with anyone, including the media, other than their counsel and immediate members of the accused's family; (j) not to occupy any official position within Bosnia-Herzegovina; (k) to report to the Registrar of the Tribunal within three days of the start of employment, the position occupied, as well as the name and address of the employer; (l) to comply strictly with any requirements of the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina necessary to enable them to comply with their obligations under the order for provisional release and their guarantees; (m) to return to the Tribunal at such time and on such date as the Trial Chamber may order; (n) to comply strictly with any order of the Trial Chamber wherein the terms of or terminating the provisional release of the accused. Requires the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina to assume responsibility for: (a) all expenses concerning transport of the accused from Schiphol airport to their place of residence and back, and; (b) the personal security and safety of the accused while on provisional release; (c) reporting immediately to the Registrar of the Tribunal the substance of any threats to the security of the accused, including full reports of investigations related to such threats at the request of the Trial Chamber or of the parties; (d) facilitating all means of cooperation and communication between the parties and to ensure the confidentiality of any such communication; (e) submitting a written report to the Registrar of the Tribunal every month as to the presence of the accused and their compliance with the terms of this order; (f) immediately detaining the accused should they breach any of the terms and conditions of their provisional release and reporting immediately to the Trial Chamber any such breach; (g) respecting the primacy of the Tribunal in relation to any existing or future proceedings in Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning the accused; (h) in relation to Mehmed Alagic specifically, regardless of the outcome of any pending proceedings against him in Bosnia-Herzegovina, retransferring Mehmed Alagic to the Tribunal when requested. Instructs the Registrar of the Tribunal to consult with the Ministry of Justice of the Netherlands and the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina as to the practical arrangement for the release of the accused. Requests the authorities of all states through which the accused will travel to hold the accused in custody for any time they will spend in transit at the airport and to detain and to arrest the accused pending their return to the United Nations Detention Unit, should they intend to escape. I would ask the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you understand this order and are you ready to comply with this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have completely understood the order of the Trial Chamber, and we accept to comply with this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIMOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should also like to confirm that we accept the order as presented by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzihasanovic, would you please rise. Are you ready to comply with the order you just heard? THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] I'm completely ready to comply with the order, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am completely ready to comply with the order read out, and all its provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I take this as your word of honour. Mr. Kubura, please rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My word of honour, you have. It. THE ACCUSED KUBURA: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall completely comply with the order issued by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I have no interpretation. THE ACCUSED KUBURA: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I completely comply with the order issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I take this as your word of honour. And Mr. Alagic, please rise. THE ACCUSED ALAGIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to thank you for your decision and ruling, and I shall fully comply with the order issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take this as your word of honour. THE ACCUSED ALAGIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. All the parties and public will receive, of course, the three decisions with the reasoning in writing without delay. Just to give you some reasons in short, first of all, I want to point out, especially addressing you, the three accused, that this decision doesn't change your situation as accused in this Tribunal at all. There is still the trial of serious -- and the indictment of very serious crimes committed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and it is by no way any kind of decision on the merits of this indictment. It's just in respect to human rights that we have to follow the discretion given us by Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY and the underlying issues of human rights. These general human rights enshrined in our Statute in matters of detention on remand are such that detention should be the exception, release should be the rule, and any kind of remand should be as short as possible so as not to amount to punishment in disguise, as it would infringe the presumption of innocence. We know that these Rules have been conceived for criminal investigations and trials before national authorities. They're more difficult to apply on the international level. International criminal courts and tribunals have no police forces at their disposal to re-arrest released detainees who have absconded. Alleged war crimes are particularly complex and long to investigate, and the crimes are, of course -- each case is a very serious one, and the release of a suspect may in principle - I emphasise "in principle" - create high risk for witnesses and victims. In the practice of the ICTY, this has meant de facto - and once again, I emphasise "de facto" - continued detention of suspects and accused was the rule, rather than the exception. However, Rule 65 provides for provisional release and gives some discretion to the Trial Chambers. This discretion has to be exercised. It has not to be exercised in general terms but with regard to each single individual person. When applying this Rule, first of all, on the basis of the facts submitted to and available for the Trial Chamber, we regard the behaviour of each of the accused as a voluntary surrender. What else should they have done, especially regarding Mr. Kubura, returning from holiday in Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina? If he would -- if he intended to flee, it would be an easy exercise to go in any other direction in the world than return to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Applying the principle of proportionality, the test is whether or not the arrest, continued arrest, is really necessary or can the same goal be achieved by other less-intrusive measures? The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the above-mentioned strict orders - even stricter than those suggested by the Office of the Prosecutor - fulfil this purpose in a proper manner. We have documents by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from the three accused giving us certain guarantees meeting the expectation of this Trial Chamber. We are, of course, aware that there never can be a total guarantee, but there is a sufficient basis. We took into consideration the submissions of the parties, but found that as regards the guarantees, there was no necessity, on the one hand, to be more lenient or, on the other hand, to give more strict orders. This is, in short, the underlying reason of our decision, and as mentioned before, we will issue as soon as possible the decision in writing. The main issue, once again, we rely on you, and we expect you to be here whenever it is demanded and respect all the other orders. Any other submissions right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has no observations to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So following the rules of logic, I regard it as given that there is no request for a stay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this conclusion is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There's no --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's correct. It's the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Ladies and gentlemen, so I can thank you for the good cooperation during the last month on this case. I would like to extend Season's Greetings to all present, especially those normally working behind the scenes, and at the same time express my gratitude for the interpreters for providing a common basis of understanding. Hereby this hearing is concluded.
